newsitem.title: GERMANY: Top German guerrilla suspect gives himself up.
newsitem.headline: Top German guerrilla suspect gives himself up.

text.p: The top suspect in one of Germany's most spectacular political killings turned himself in on Friday after pleading his innocence in a press interview earlier this month, justice officials said.

Christoph Seidler, wanted for the 1989 car-bomb killing of Deutsche Bank chief executive Alfred Herrhausen, was promptly handed over to an investigating judge for interrogation, the Federal Prosecutor's office said.
A spokesman said the office would not comment further until the questioning ended later in the day.
Seidler, now 38, is one of the last members of the Red Army Faction (RAF) who was still at large.
He says he was in Lebanon at the time of the Herrhausen assassination, which shook Germany only weeks after the burst of euphoria following the fall of the Berlin Wall.
Seidler told Der Spiegel magazine early this month that he hoped to clear his name by turning himself in.
He acknowledged links with the RAF, once known as the Baader-Meinhof Gang, in the 1980s but added: "I never had anything to do with any RAF operation in concrete terms."

Seidler, whose face appears on wanted posters in every post office and police station in Germany, made contact last year with the anti-extremist Office for the Protection of the Constitution to present evidence in his defence.

He said he hoped the end of the emotionally and politically charged atmosphere of the 1970s and 1980s, when the RAF was battling the German establishment with spectacular killings and abductions, would now allow him a fair hearing.

The attacks of the 1970s and 1980s, carried out at a time of left-wing intellectual ferment and the East-West tension of the superpower arms race, claimed over 50 lives and forced Germany to turn its institutions into virtual fortresses.

Many former RAF leaders have now been released or pardoned. All the nine who remain in jail now reject the use of violence for political ends, even if it is hardly out of affection for the system on which they had declared war.
